pages.title: About Robin
pages.content:
Hello, I am Robin

I spent twelve years as an analyst and designer in small organisations where nobody had time for a three-day training course. Atlas Academy is the course I wish I had been given: short, practical and kind.

Every lesson is recorded in my spare room studio, tested on real students and rewritten until it is as short as it can be.

What I believe about learning

  • Adults learn best from problems they actually have.
  • Ten focused minutes beat an hour of half-watching.
  • Feedback should be specific, kind and quick.

Robin explains things like a colleague who wants you to succeed, not a lecturer.

A Clear Writing student

The small print

Atlas Academy is independent: no investors, no adverts, no selling your data. Courses are paid for by students, and a share of every enrolment funds free places for people on low incomes.

posts.title: Five Spreadsheet Formulas That Save Hours Every Week
posts.excerpt: You do not need to be a numbers person. These five formulas cover most of the copying, counting and tidying people do by hand.
posts.content:
Most of the time we lose in spreadsheets is not spent on hard maths. It is spent copying, counting, tidying and looking things up by hand. Five formulas cover nearly all of it, and you can learn them before your coffee goes cold.

The five

A worked example

Imagine a sheet of expenses with a category in column B and an amount in column C. To total everything in the Travel category, type this into any empty cell:

=SUMIF(B2:B200, "Travel", C2:C200)

Change the word in quotes to total another category, or point it at a cell that holds the category name so you can build a whole summary table in a minute.

Learn the formula once, then let the spreadsheet do the boring part forever.

Lesson 3, Data Basics

Try each formula on a copy of a real sheet from your own work. That is the fastest way to make it stick, and it is exactly how the Data Basics course is built.

comments.author: Lena
comments.content: XLOOKUP just replaced about forty minutes of my Monday. Thank you!

comments.author: Kofi
comments.content: Is there a version of SUMIF that takes two conditions?

posts.title: A Beginner's Guide to Colour for Non-Designers
posts.excerpt: One main colour, one accent and plenty of neutrals. A simple system for slides, posters and websites that look calm and confident.
posts.content:
Colour feels like the most mysterious part of design, but most good layouts follow a simple recipe: one main colour, one accent and plenty of neutral space in between.

The 60-30-10 rule

  • 60% neutral: backgrounds, white space, body text.
  • 30% main colour: headings, panels, navigation.
  • 10% accent: buttons, highlights, the one thing you want clicked.

The accent works because it is rare. The moment everything is highlighted, nothing is.

Check your contrast

Pale grey text on white looks elegant on a big monitor and disappears on a phone in sunlight. Aim for dark text on light backgrounds, and test anything important with a contrast checker before you publish.

comments.author: Mira
comments.content: The 60-30-10 rule fixed my team's slide deck in an afternoon.

posts.title: How to Outline a Long Essay Without Losing the Thread
posts.excerpt: A blank page is terrifying; a good outline is not. A four-step method for turning scattered notes into a clear argument.
posts.content:
Long essays rarely go wrong in the sentences. They go wrong in the structure: a brilliant paragraph in the wrong place, or an argument that drifts until the conclusion has nothing to conclude.

Four steps

  1. Write the answer first. One sentence that states what you think and why.
  2. List the reasons. Three to five claims that support that sentence.
  3. Attach the evidence. Under each claim, note the quotes, data or examples you will use.
  4. Order for the reader. Start with the claim they will accept most easily.

Your outline is not a contract. If you discover a better argument while writing, change the answer sentence and reshuffle. That is the outline doing its job.

Before

Twenty pages of notes, a vague topic and a deadline on Friday.

After

One answer sentence, four claims, twelve pieces of evidence and a plan for each section.

The Clear Writing course includes a printable outline template and walks through three real essays from first note to final draft.

posts.title: A Learning Plan Template You Will Actually Use
posts.excerpt: Most learning plans are too ambitious by Wednesday. This one fits on a single page and survives a busy month.
posts.content:
Ambitious learning plans have a short life. They start on a Monday with two hours a day and quietly die on Thursday. The plan below is deliberately modest, which is exactly why it lasts.

The one-page plan

Put the plan somewhere you will see it daily. Tick off sessions on a calendar: a chain of ticks is surprisingly motivating, and a gap is an honest reminder rather than a failure.

Twenty-five minutes three times a week beats a heroic weekend you never repeat.

Every Atlas course ends each module with a suggested plan for the next four weeks, so you never have to start from a blank page.

posts.title: Student Story: From Night Shifts to Data Analyst
posts.excerpt: A warehouse supervisor took Data Basics in twenty-minute breaks. Eighteen months later, she builds the dashboards her old team uses.
posts.content:
When Jo enrolled in Data Basics she was supervising night shifts at a distribution warehouse, studying in twenty-minute breaks on her phone and a borrowed laptop.

I did not think of myself as a numbers person. I just knew the spreadsheets we used were wasting everyone's time.

Jo, Data Basics graduate

What changed

Her course project was a simple sheet that tracked late deliveries by route. Her manager used it in a meeting the following week, and within a month she was asked to build a version for the whole site.

  • Course finished in eleven weeks
  • Three projects built on real work data
  • Promoted to operations analyst eighteen months later

Jo now mentors new students in the community forum. Her advice for beginners: pick a problem from your own job and solve it badly first, then better.

posts.title: Study Habits That Stick (and Three That Do Not)
posts.excerpt: Re-reading and highlighting feel productive but barely work. Here is what the evidence says helps adults learn and remember.
posts.content:
Adult learners are busy, tired and often learning something that matters for their job. That makes it worth spending study time on the methods that work, not just the ones that feel productive.

Do more of

  • Testing yourself without notes
  • Spacing sessions across days
  • Mixing different kinds of problems
  • Explaining an idea out loud

Do less of

  • Re-reading the same chapter
  • Highlighting whole pages
  • Cramming the night before

Testing yourself is uncomfortable because you notice what you have forgotten. That discomfort is the learning happening.

Try it this week

At the end of each lesson, close the video and write down the three most important points from memory. Check them the next day. That single habit will do more than an extra hour of watching.

posts.title: Charts That Tell the Truth
posts.excerpt: Cropped axes, crowded pies and rainbow colours can mislead even when every number is right. Five checks before you share a chart.
posts.content:
A chart can be built from perfectly accurate numbers and still leave the reader with the wrong idea. Usually it is not deliberate: it is the default settings doing the thinking.

Five checks

  1. Does a bar chart start its axis at zero?
  2. Could the pie be a sorted bar chart instead?
  3. Is colour used to highlight one thing, not to decorate?
  4. Does the title say what the reader should notice?
  5. Would the chart still make sense printed in grey?

Most charting tools will happily produce a 3D exploding pie with twelve slices. Just because a setting exists does not mean the reader benefits from it.

Good charts are a kindness to the reader. They answer the question "so what?" before anyone has to ask it.

comments.author: Priyanka
comments.content: Check number five is brilliant. Half our reports fail it.
